slides.title: The Attribution Framework shows the white space.
slides.headline: The Attribution Framework shows the white space.
slides.support: It compares your whole company with your competitors, across your market.
body: Where does everyone compete on the same thing?
Where is the white space, where nobody competes yet?
Where will you be in three years?
notes: Strategy is a unique and valuable position. You get there by moving into white space that matters to your Core Customer.
This is about the company, not a product.
It is a key strategic picture. Give it time, and let the team sleep on it.
Allow about 60 minutes.

slides.title: Attribution Framework example
slides.headline: Attribution Framework example
notes: The same subscription company, with three competitors from its Market Map.
Competitor A sells through app marketplaces. Competitor B sells to larger companies through resellers. Competitor C is the low-cost option.
Walk the graph once. The next slides take each part in turn.
The scores are directional. Do not argue a 3 against a 4.
Point at a name in the legend, or click it, to show that line on its own.

Scores run from 1 to 5. Five lines: Us today, Competitor A, Competitor B, Competitor C and the 3HAG line. Us today runs from 4 on the left to 2 on the right. The 3HAG line rises to 5 on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person, and drops on reporting and customization.

slides.title: Attributes: how everyone on your Market Map compares companies.
slides.headline: Attributes: how everyone on your Market Map compares companies.
notes: An attribute is something the market compares companies on.
Anyone with power on your Market Map weighs attributes: buyers, channels, influencers and acquirers.
Include attributes nobody competes on yet. No customer can ask for those.
Keep it at company level. Do not list product features.
Aim for 12 to 15 attributes.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom, ordered from the one the company serves best: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. Every line is dimmed and the attribute names are bright. Callout: Why: the market sets the attributes, not our product. Ask: what describes the whole market?

slides.title: Example: the company scores itself, 1 to 5.
slides.headline: Example: the company scores itself, 1 to 5.
notes: Score how well the company serves each attribute today, from 1 to 5.
Order the attributes from best to worst. The line then falls from left to right.
Score today honestly. A company with no 5s has room to grow.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom, ordered from the one the company serves best: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. Every line is dimmed except Us today, which falls from 4 on the left to 2 on the right. Callout: Why: an honest score shows where we stand today. Ask: how well do we serve each attribute, 1 to 5?

slides.title: Example: the top competitors, on the same attributes.
slides.headline: Example: the top competitors, on the same attributes.
notes: Score two or three competitors on the same attributes, in the same order.
If the team cannot score a competitor with confidence, stop. Assign the research as homework.
Look for where every line bunches together. That is where everyone competes on the same thing.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom, ordered from the one the company serves best: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. Us today is dimmed. The 3HAG line is not shown. The three competitor lines are bright: A is strongest on integrations, B on feature breadth, customization and partner network, C is low almost everywhere. Callout: Why: the lines show where everyone competes. Ask: how would each competitor score?

slides.title: White space is where nothing is drawn.
slides.headline: White space is where nothing is drawn.
notes: White space is any part of the graph with nothing in it. It can sit above the lines or below them.
In the example, nobody scores a 5 on speed of setup, price predictability or support from a person.
Ask the team where the white space is before you point at it.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom, ordered from the one the company serves best: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. Us today and the three competitor lines are dimmed, on a grey ground. The 3HAG line is not shown. The empty area above the lines is left white, with a dashed outline. Callout: Why: white space is a position with no rivals. Ask: where on the graph is nothing drawn?

slides.title: The 3HAG line is where you will be in three years.
slides.headline: The 3HAG line is where you will be in three years.
notes: Decide what to maintain, what to improve and what to let drop.
A good 3HAG line gives something up. If every score goes up, go again. Do not force it on the first round.
Competitors can copy what you add. They cannot copy what you drop without breaking their own business.
In the example, reporting and customization drop, so that setup, price and support can lead.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom, ordered from the one the company serves best: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. Every line is dimmed except the 3HAG line, which rises to 5 on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person and drops to 2 on reporting and 1 on customization. The white space above the other lines is left white on a grey ground, and the part the 3HAG line moves into is shaded green. Callout: Why: a real position means trade-offs. Ask: what could we afford not to be as good at?

slides.title: What are the attributes of your market?
slides.headline: What are the attributes of your market?
slides.support: Start from your Market Map: buyers, channels, influencers and acquirers.
body: On your own, write 5 to 7 things your market compares companies on.
Share them. Group the ones that mean the same thing, and name each group.
Finish with 12 to 15 attributes for the whole team.
notes: Each leader works in private. Reveal when everyone is done.
In a small team, each person writes 7 to 10, so the team still ends with 12 to 15 after grouping.
Keep the attributes about the whole market, not one customer.
Think beyond the buyer. Channels, influencers and acquirers weigh attributes too.
Allow about 20 minutes.

slides.title: Score your company and your competitors.
slides.headline: Score your company and your competitors.
slides.support: One person copies the Attribution Map sheet and enters your attributes.
body: Score your company and two or three competitors, 1 to 5.
Everyone scores alone first. The CEO shares last.
Enter the agreed scores. The graph sorts itself.
Then ask: where is the white space?
notes: Scan the code, then choose File and Make a copy in Google Sheets. One person shares the copy on screen.
Each leader writes scores in private. Then compare them, and the CEO shares last.
The spread between scores is where the discussion is.
Enter scores in any order. The sheet orders the attributes from best to worst.
The first pass is directional. Do not argue decimals.
Then ask: where is the white space?
Allow about 25 minutes.

artwork.alt: One QR code. Attribution Map sheet: make a copy, then enter your scores. It opens the Attribution Map master sheet in Google Sheets.

The sheet names the competitors 1, 2 and 3. They are Competitors A, B and C on the Market Map.
Leave the 3HAG Line column empty for now. The team fills it in when it draws the 3HAG line.
Enter the attributes in any order. The sheet sorts them from best to worst for the chart.

slides.title: Draw your 3HAG line.
slides.headline: Draw your 3HAG line.
slides.support: Decide what to maintain, what to improve and what to let drop.
body: Enter a 3HAG score for each attribute.
Ask: what will we be worse at in three years?
notes: The white space only counts if it matters to the Core Customer.
In the example, Dana needs fast setup, a predictable cost and a person to call. The 3HAG line leads on all three.
Let the team sleep on it. The line can change before the annual.
Homework: add the Attribution Framework to the War Room in Metronome.

slides.title: What does the white space change?
slides.headline: What does the white space change?
body: What should become a priority next quarter?
What will you stop doing because the 3HAG line drops it?
notes: Write the answers on the board. They become candidates when the team builds the QHAG.
Next, test the 3HAG and the 1HAG with these answers, then build the QHAG.
A team that runs out of time finishes the Attribution Framework in an extra session before the annual.
